![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14220202/assets/fa58c9d1c0680dd94bb25c04e0a268df836e14bfb217f0a20d3bd75224cec4e8.png)

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above).
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{({e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{2\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The growth rate of a watermelon production $P(t)$ in a certain land is jointly proportional to the watermelon production at time $t,$ measured in months, and the difference between the land's carrying capacity and the watermelon production. If the constant of proportionality is $0.2$ and the maximum possible watermelon production is $1\,800,$ which differential equation could be used to model $P(t)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the watermelon production growth rate is *jointly* proportional to the watermelon production at time $t$ and the difference between the carrying capacity and the watermelon production, the watermelon production follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.2,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=1\,800.$ Therefore, the watermelon production is given by the equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.2P(1\,800-P).
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{5}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5} \\ {v}^{′}=2x\, & ⟹\,v=\int 2x\,\text{d}x={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{log}_{5}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡(x)({x}^{2})-\int ({x}^{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{log}_{5}⁡(x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{log}_{5}⁡(x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{5}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={cos}^{3}⁡t,\,y={sin}^{3}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{3}⁡t)=3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t)}^{2}+{(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{4}⁡t+9{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\cdot |3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t|\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The exact global minimum value of the function $f(x)={x}^{2}-4x+5$ on the closed interval $0\le x\le 5$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)={x}^{2}-4x+5,$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=2x-4.
$$

Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4 & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the critical points are $x=2$ and the endpoints $x=0,5$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints)

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & ={0}^{2}-4(0)+5=5 \\ f(2) & ={2}^{2}-4(2)+5=1 \\ f(5) & ={5}^{2}-4(5)+5=10\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The smallest value is $f(2)=1,$ so the global minimum is $1.$

- The greatest value is $f(5)=10,$ so the global maximum is $10.$

questions.problem:
A triangle $S$ has vertices at $(0,0),(2,0),(2,2).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of ${S}^{′},$ the image of $S$ under the counterclockwise rotation ${R}_{{270}^{∘}}$ by an angle of ${270}^{∘}$ about the origin?

I. $(0,0)$

II. $(2,-2)$

III. $(-2,0)$
questions.worked_solution:
The counterclockwise rotation ${R}_{{270}^{∘}}$ by an angle of ${270}^{∘}$ is given by the matrix

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the image of $S$ under the action of ${R}_{{270}^{∘}},$ we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under ${R}_{{270}^{∘}}$ by calculating the matrix product $RX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}RX & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of ${S}^{′}$ are $(0,0),(0,-2),(2,-2).$

So, the correct answer is "I and II only."
